newsitem.title: USA: Hubble telescope flies free of U.S. shuttle.
newsitem.headline: Hubble telescope flies free of U.S. shuttle.

text.p: The crew of the space shuttle Discovery released the Hubble Space Telescope on Wednesday after a $350 million refurbishment that left the observatory with better eyes to probe the universe.

The four-story silver telescope, with golden wings of solar cells, flew free of Discovery's robot arm at 1:41 a.m. EST (0641 GMT) as the two craft soared 385 miles (620 km) up approaching the west coast of Africa.
Hubble "is free to study the stars," radioed shuttle commander Ken Bowersox as he backed away the 250,000 pound (115,000 kg) spaceship.

Astronaut Steve Hawley had used the 50-foot (15 metre)-long mechanical limb to raise the telescope from its dry dock in the shuttle's cargo bay, where astronauts had spent about 33 hours outside upgrading its ageing instruments and components.
Discovery left the telescope orbiting 9 miles (15 km) higher than when it picked it up. Four boosts with the shuttle's precision manoeuvring jets had nudged the telescope hight

During the shuttle's service call, two teams of spacewalking astronauts made five spacewalks to fit the $2 billion orbiting observatory with an improved light-splitting spectrograph to seek out black holes and an infrared camera package capable of peering through veils of dust.

"These are all instruments built in 1990's with today's technology and far surpass anything we have on the old space telescope," Ed Weiler, Hubble's chief astronomer said. "We just don't know what we're going to see with these new instruments."
The shuttle crew also dabbled in electronic brain surgery, installing a new control box for the telescope's solar arrays and a relay system for its computers.

The telescope's peeled, sunburned skin called for some unexpected repairs. A fifth spacewalk was added to the mission to patch up the tears in the observatory's reflective foil skin, which protects it from the extreme temperatures in orbit.
Engineers at mission control in Houston quickly devised ways of lashing improvised sunshades over the torn and tattered areas using tie wraps, electical wire and parachute cord.
"There was nothing thrown at us that we couldn't handle," spacewalker Greg Harbaugh told CNN on Wednesday.
"From my viewpoint, we did more than we set out to do," John Campbell, a Hubble manager, said. "I'd say we're 110 percent successful."

If all goes according to plan, the telescope should restart observations in three or four weeks, Weiler said. The first images and data from its new instruments should be beamed back to earth in about 10 weeks.
A shuttle crew will return to Hubble in December 1999 to install another new instrument, replace its electricity-generating solar panels and better patch up its tattered thermal insulation.
Astronomers hope regular service calls will keep the telescope running until 2005.
Discovery was due to return to earth on Friday, making a rare nighttime landing at Florida's Kennedy Space Centre.
